title: H-1B Registrations Plunge 38.5% as Wage-Weighted System Reshapes Program
excerpt: FY2027 registrations fell from 343,981 to 211,600 — the lowest in seven years — as Indian IT firms pull back on fresh filings amid tougher rules and a $100,000 fee.
body:
• H-1B registrations dropped 38.5% in FY2027, from 343,981 to 211,600, the lowest level in seven years, according to USCIS data.
  • 71.5% of selected applicants hold a US master's degree or higher, up from 57% a year earlier, reflecting the new wage-weighted selection system.
  • Indian IT firms are pulling back on fresh H-1B filings as the $100,000 fee and stricter enforcement make sponsorship economics increasingly difficult.

New H-1B visa registrations plummeted 38.5 percent for fiscal year 2027, falling from 343,981 to just 211,600, according to US Citizenship and Immigration Services data released in May. The decline marks the lowest registration level in seven years and signals a fundamental shift in how employers approach the program.

USCIS attributed the drop to changes in the selection system that reduced incentives for mass, low-wage registrations rather than a decline in employer demand for foreign talent. The annual cap of 85,000 visas — 65,000 regular plus 20,000 for US advanced degree holders — remains oversubscribed despite the sharper decline.

Higher Wages, Higher Degrees

The data reflects the impact of a wage-weighted selection system that took effect on February 27, 2026, replacing the random lottery. Under the new rules, applicants in higher wage categories receive more entries: Wage Level IV gets four entries, Level III gets three, Level II gets two, and Level I gets one.

The results are stark. An overwhelming 71.5 percent of selected applicants hold a US master's degree or higher, up from 57 percent last year. Only 17.7 percent of selected registrations fell in the lowest wage category.

"This data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the programme with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the programme is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers."

— USCIS statement

Indian IT Companies Pull Back

The decline carries outsized implications for the Indian technology sector. Indians make up an estimated 71 percent of all approved H-1B applications in recent years, and Indian IT services firms have historically been among the program's heaviest users.

Data from the National Foundation for American Policy showed that new-hire H-1B approvals for the top seven Indian IT firms had already fallen 37 percent in FY2025 to just 4,573 — a decade low. Tata Consultancy Services remained the only Indian company in the top five H-1B employers, with Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Google occupying the first four slots for the first time.

Industry analysts point to three converging forces driving the retreat. First, the $100,000 fee imposed by a September 2025 presidential proclamation made fresh sponsorship prohibitively expensive for many employers. A company filing 5,000 H-1B petitions would face $500 million in fees alone.

Second, Indian IT vendors have expanded nearshore delivery centers in Canada, Mexico, and Eastern Europe, reducing dependence on US work permits. Third, firms increasingly reserve H-1B slots for extensions of existing employees rather than new hires.

The Fee Factor

The $100,000 per-petition fee, which applies to certain new filings after September 2025, has fundamentally altered the economics of H-1B sponsorship. A federal court struck down the fee in June 2026, but the administration has said it will appeal, leaving employers in limbo.

Nasscom, the Indian IT industry body, welcomed a US clarification that the fee would not affect current visa holders and would apply only as a one-time charge on fresh petitions. But the uncertainty has already pushed companies to accelerate local hiring in the United States.

What This Means for Indian Professionals

For Indian professionals seeking new H-1B sponsorship, the math has shifted significantly. The wage-weighted system favors higher-paid roles, and the registration window — which ran from March 4 to March 19, 2026 — saw no second lottery. Unselected workers must wait until the FY2028 registration period, expected in March 2027.

Those already in the US on H-1B status face a different but related pressure. Extension denial rates have edged up, and USCIS enhanced background checks are causing processing delays for green card and naturalization cases nationwide.

The shift underscores a broader realignment in how Indian talent reaches the American labor market, with advanced degrees, higher salaries, and US-based credentials becoming the primary path through an increasingly selective system.

nri_angle: Indians make up 71% of H-1B holders and face a dramatically reshaped selection system that favors US-educated, higher-paid applicants over traditional IT services placements.
